item.title: US air traffic outage lays bare infrastructure underinvestment, structural flaws in country's political system: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15 17:38:00
Passengers wait at Ontario International Airport following flight delays in Ontario, California, the United States, on November 13, 2026. The US Federal Aviation Administration lifted a nationwide ground stop on Friday evening after hours of disruption affected thousands of flights across the country. Photo: Xinhua A massive, nearly five-hour shutdown of the US aviation system that has disrupted more than 20,000 flights since Friday may have been the fault of a single router installed by government contractor L3Harris, US government officials said Saturday, Reuters reported, calling the incident the latest and most dramatic sign of strain on a US air traffic control system. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told a news conference on Saturday local time that a contractor for the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) was working at a remote location to replace a copper line when an unknown issue overloaded the aging air traffic control system, forcing the FAA to keep planes on the ground nationwide, CBC News reported. Speaking at a White House news conference Friday evening, Duffy blamed outdated routers and decades-old technology for Friday's nationwide FAA ground stop, urging Congress to approve $50 billion in emergency funding to rebuild the country's aging air traffic control system, Fox Business reported. As of 6:45 pm, airlines on Saturday had canceled more than 6,150 US flights and delayed more than 7,300, according to FlightAware, an aviation website. That followed about 9,200 flights canceled and 7,500 delayed on Friday after the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop because of disruptions to air traffic communications. FlightAware said more than 530 flights scheduled for Sunday were already canceled, per Reuters. The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Friday that halted nearly all departing flights for almost five hours. It was the longest nationwide halt to air travel since the September 11, 2001, attacks and one of the single worst US travel days ever, Reuters reported. During a Saturday news conference explaining why the FAA instituted a nationwide ground stop for all flights Friday, Duffy claimed a technical issue may have occurred while federal telecommunications contractor L3Harris was doing work on an FAA telecommunications line, according to Fox Business. Duffy continued to explain that while L3Harris was upgrading the network from copper lines to fiber-optic cables, the FAA's router at that location began experiencing a flood of data causing it to be overwhelmed — an issue that quickly spread to routers at other FAA air traffic control systems nationwide, Fox Business reported. Duffy blamed Congress for failing to fund a new system that he said could prevent such outages and called for $50 billion US to modernize it. Earlier on Friday, before the outage, the White House and US Department of Transportation had urged Congress to approve $30.1 billion to upgrade the nation's aging airports and air traffic control infrastructure, according to CBC News. According to Wang Hao, a professor at Fudan University's Center for American Studies, aging US infrastructure reflects not only underinvestment and slow technological upgrades but also deeper structural problems within the country's political system. On the one hand, the division of responsibilities and authority among federal, state and local governments under the US federal system, coupled with deepening partisan polarization, makes it difficult to build a stable consensus on long-term infrastructure investment. On the other hand, the influence of interest groups on policymaking and regulatory processes has led some industries to favor protecting their existing interests rather than proactively shouldering the costs of safety upgrades and technological modernization, Wang told the Global Times on Sunday. Hong Kong's Cathay Pacific Airways issued a statement on Saturday that due to the nationwide ground stop previously issued by the US FAA, all flights to and from the US were affected. Two Cathay Pacific flights departing from the US on November 13 local time (CX807 and CX879) were delayed as a result of the restrictions. The airline arranged hotel accommodation for affected passengers. Zheng Hongfeng, CEO of industry information provider VariFlight, told the Global Times on Sunday that the incident temporarily grounded flights, but the disruption affected a relatively wide area. According to Zheng, the disruption, which affected US nationwide flight operations for more than four hours, underscores the critical role of digital system security and reliability in national aviation operations, highlighting the need for increased investment in digital infrastructure as the industry enters the AI era. The civil aviation industry is facing new operational challenges that require technological solutions. This is a new issue confronting aviation professionals worldwide, Zheng said.

item.title: Xi's article on jointly building Asia-Pacific community with shared future to be published
item.description:

CHINA / POLITICS Xi's article on jointly building Asia-Pacific community with shared future to be published By Xinhua Published: Nov 15, 2026 05:22 PM
An article by Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, on jointly building an Asia-Pacific community with a shared future will be published on Monday. The article by Xi, also Chinese president and chairman of the Central Military Commission, will be published in this year's 22nd issue of the Qiushi Journal, a flagship magazine of the CPC Central Committee. It is a compilation of excerpts from Xi's important remarks on the subject made between October 2013 and November 2025.

item.title: 115 Fortune Global 500 companies to attend APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15 14:20:00
This photo taken on Nov. 3, 2026 shows an APEC-themed installation at a park in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. China will hold the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen from Nov. 18 to 19. (Xinhua/Mao Siqian) A total of 115 Fortune Global 500 companies will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) CEO Summit 2026, scheduled for November 17-18 in South China's Shenzhen, the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade (CCPIT) said at a press briefing on Sunday. Li Qingshuang, vice chairman of the CCPIT, said at the event that US participants make up the largest group from economies other than China, accounting for nearly 20 percent of the total. Heads of several international organizations and business associations from the US, Russia, Japan and other economies will also be on site to join the gathering. At the fourth meeting of the APEC Business Advisory Council (ABAC), Chinese representatives put forward proposals on artificial intelligence (AI) applications, zero-carbon transport, cross-border QR-code payments, green agriculture and supply-chain cooperation, according to Wu Meng, head of the international department of the CCPIT. And, Chinese representatives worked with US business representatives on a joint proposal to strengthen Asia-Pacific supply-chain cooperation, and with Canadian business representatives on an "AI plus" joint proposal - pushing the initiatives from concepts into concrete business action and deepening the substance of APEC's business agenda. Wu noted that a Chinese proposal to set up a connectivity working group - revived after an eight-year hiatus - has won broad support, reflecting a clear consensus among Asia-Pacific businesses on strengthening regional infrastructure and institutional connectivity, the Securities Times reported. Xu Liang, deputy secretary-general of the China Chamber of International Commerce, said more than 130 representative Shenzhen-based companies from various sectors will join the summit, with several local tech and manufacturing leaders invited to panel discussions on cooperation with the broader APEC business community. In the first three quarters of 2026, Shenzhen's trade with other APEC economies reached 3.23 trillion yuan ($484 billion), up 40 percent year on year - leading all Chinese mainland cities and underscoring the city's long-term footprint in the Asia-Pacific market. Under the theme "To Prosper and Win the Future Together", government and business representatives from APEC economies will gather at the upcoming summit to exchange views on major issues, including the building of the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific (FTAAP), connectivity, AI, digital economy, the development of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, and sustainable development, and offer insights and recommendations for promoting economic growth across the Asia-Pacific region. The APEC CEO Summit 2026 will bring together around 1,000 delegates. And, representatives from Asia-Pacific business communities have expressed high hopes for this week's events in Shenzhen. "Our experience shows how open trade, stable relationships and mutually beneficial cooperation can create lasting value for participating economies and contribute to shared prosperity across the APEC region," Teh-han Chow, CEO of Greater China of New Zealand dairy giant Fonterra, told the Global Times on Sunday. "At our Edendale site in New Zealand, for example, an electric boiler manufactured in China has replaced coal-fired equipment, significantly reducing emissions from milk processing," Chow said.

item.title: Nvidia succession turmoil: Politics at the wheel turns innovation and commercial value into collateral damage, Chinese experts warn
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15 13:11:00
Nvidia Photo: VCG Nvidia's struggle to chart a succession path after the departure of founder and CEO Jensen Huang has exposed a deeper problem facing the US tech industry: As political pressures increasingly spill into corporate affairs, even the world's most successful technology companies could find it harder to safeguard management stability, strategic autonomy and the conditions needed for innovation, Chinese experts said. The uncertainty has spread from the boardroom to the stock market and the company's workforce. Nvidia shares have recorded six straight weeks of declines, their longest losing streak since October 2012, read a Reuters report. Meanwhile, a public petition calling for Huang's reinstatement had attracted more than 108,000 signatures by Saturday, according to a US-based news outlet Business Insider, reflecting growing support for the former CEO beyond the company's workforce. The leadership succession question took another turn after the Financial Times reported on Friday that Nvidia's board had approached Arm CEO Rene Haas as a potential candidate. Haas spent seven years at Nvidia, rising to vice president and general manager of its computing products business, before joining Arm in 2013. Nvidia's board subsequently said it was selecting a search firm and had not formally approached any potential candidates, adding that speculation about individual candidates was premature. CFO Colette Kress is currently serving as interim CEO, according to the company's official statement. The developments highlight a fundamental challenge for Nvidia: How to replace a founder whose influence has extended far beyond executive management. Zhou Mi, a senior research fellow at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation, told the Global Times that Nvidia's development had largely revolved around Huang, leaving its corporate governance structure vulnerable to disruption should its central figure suddenly depart. The change has brought considerable uncertainty to the company's operations, business performance and investor expectations, Zhou said. Xiang Ligang, director-general of the Zhongguancun Modern Information Consumer Application Industry Technology Alliance, said Huang had led Nvidia for more than three decades, transforming it from a relatively small chipmaker into one of the world's most valuable technology companies. Particularly during the recent AI boom, Huang played an indispensable role in shaping the company's technology roadmap, strategic planning and long-term development. Nvidia had not established a clear successor capable of independently assuming Huang's role in long-term strategic decision-making, Xiang said. His departure therefore represents more than a routine executive reshuffle, potentially leaving the company temporarily without a clear strategic center. This helps explain why some employees are calling for Huang's return, he said. Yet the succession challenge also raises broader questions about the political environment in which US technology companies operate. Huang's departure came after a period of heightened media scrutiny in the US, with some Western media reports drawing connections between controversies surrounding his private life and politically charged allegations of alleged links to the "China spy." Although Beijing has firmly rejected the "Chinese spy" narrative, stressing that China's sci-tech progress relies on independent innovation and open cooperation, and urged Washington to stop fabricating such narratives as a pretext for imposing technology restrictions, the smear campaign continues to cast a shadow over Nvidia's corporate governance and future development. Xiang said the circumstances and timing surrounding the controversies preceding Huang's departure deserved closer scrutiny. He noted that the issue could involve political and commercial interests beyond an ordinary corporate management dispute, although the possibility of political involvement should not be confused with an established finding. As one of the few companies to have translated surging AI demand into substantial revenue and profits, Nvidia occupies a pivotal position in the global AI supply chain. Its leadership uncertainty could therefore have repercussions well beyond the company itself. "The increasingly restrictive policy environment facing US technology companies had introduced additional uncertainty into their business decisions," Zhou said. With different voices in the US government advocating varying degrees of regulation and intervention, companies could find themselves having to assess political risks alongside market demand and technological feasibility, he added. This shift in decision-making priorities could undermine the foundations of technological innovation, Zhou said. When companies devote more attention to anticipating political developments and regulatory changes, their willingness to undertake risks and invest in uncertain technological breakthroughs may diminish. Policy uncertainty can also increase the potential costs and losses associated with innovation, while affecting corporate operations and the movement of talent, he noted. The implications also extend to global business cooperation. China remains an important market for the global semiconductor and AI industries, and the ability of companies such as Nvidia to pursue normal commercial cooperation across markets depends heavily on a stable and predictable policy environment. Business decisions should be guided by market demand, technological development and commercial interests - not political calculations. For Nvidia, its future leadership arrangements will ultimately be a corporate decision. But maintaining healthy and mutually beneficial business ties with China would also serve the company's long-term interests. More broadly, stable China-US economic and technological cooperation requires businesses to be able to make decisions on commercial grounds, without unnecessary political interference, Chinese experts noted.

item.title: Art exhibition showcases Chinese and Pakistani cultural heritage, deepening friendship
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15 07:54:00
Visitors paint patterns on porcelain during an art exhibition celebrating the 75th anniversary of Pakistan-China diplomatic relations in Islamabad, capital of Pakistan, on Nov. 12, 2026. (Xinhua/Ahmad Kamal) Students visit an art exhibition celebrating the 75th anniversary of Pakistan-China diplomatic relations in Islamabad, capital of Pakistan, on Nov. 12, 2026. (Xinhua/Ahmad Kamal) A student visits an art exhibition celebrating the 75th anniversary of Pakistan-China diplomatic relations in Islamabad, capital of Pakistan, on Nov. 12, 2026. (Xinhua/Ahmad Kamal) Students visit an art exhibition celebrating the 75th anniversary of Pakistan-China diplomatic relations in Islamabad, capital of Pakistan, on Nov. 12, 2026. (Xinhua/Ahmad Kamal) Pakiza Zainab, an 18-year-old art student from Islamabad Model College for Girls, was immersed in observing the delicate art pieces with curiosity and admiration at an exhibition held in Islamabad, Pakistan's federal capital, to celebrate the 75th anniversary of Pakistan-China diplomatic relations. Hosted by the Islamabad Museum and the Department of Archaeology and Museums under the National Heritage and Culture Division, Government of Pakistan, together with the China Cultural Center in Pakistan, the exhibition showcased a remarkable array of Chinese porcelain treasures and contemporary artworks, highlighting a rich legacy of craftsmanship, artistic creativity and cultural exchange spanning centuries. "As a fine arts student, I am glad to be here today at this wonderful exhibition featuring art collections from Pakistan and China. This is an amazing initiative as it not only strengthens the friendship between the two countries but also provides an opportunity for people to appreciate and understand each other's rich cultural heritage through art," the student said. Zainab said she was particularly impressed with the craftsmanship behind Chinese porcelain artifacts, including jars, teapots and plates. "Porcelain is such a beautiful art form, and creating these pieces requires great skill, patience and dedication. The exhibition allows us to appreciate not only the beauty of the finished works but also the artistic traditions and craftsmanship that have been passed down through generations," she said. Zainab said exhibitions like this provided art students with valuable exposure. "We often study Chinese culture and Chinese art through books, but seeing these works with our own eyes is a completely different experience. I personally have a great interest in Chinese art, so it is wonderful to see such beautiful examples of Chinese craftsmanship here in Pakistan." Speaking on the occasion, Parliamentary Secretary for National Heritage and Culture Division of Pakistan Farah Naz Akbar said cultural exchanges are an important pillar of the enduring friendship between Pakistan and China, helping deepen mutual understanding and strengthen bonds between the peoples of the two countries. She expressed hope that the exhibition would encourage greater exchanges among museums, artists, researchers and cultural institutions of the two countries. "Such cooperation can help preserve cultural heritage, share knowledge and create new opportunities for people in Pakistan and China to work together," the official said, adding that friendship is strengthened through shared stories, cultural experiences and respect for each other's traditions. "As we celebrate the 75th year of diplomatic relations, let us honor the generations who have nurtured this friendship and renew our commitment to passing it on," Akbar said. Chen Peng, counselor of the Chinese Embassy in Pakistan, said China-Pakistan cultural exchanges have gradually evolved into a two-way, in-depth integration over the past 75 years since the establishment of diplomatic ties. "A series of events, including art performances, academic seminars, film and television programs, and youth exchanges, have followed one after another," he said, adding that more and more Pakistani friends have come to understand the profound depth of Chinese culture through these exhibitions and activities, while a growing number of Chinese people have developed a deep appreciation for Pakistan's unique traditional arts and culture. The exhibition was attended by officials, cultural representatives, academics, artists and students from Pakistan and China.

item.title: Developer of China's J-35 series fighter jets uses 3D printing to advance warplane structural development, building lighter, stronger aircraft
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-14 15:00:00
A J-35 stealth fighter jet is ready to take off from China's first electromagnetic catapult-equipped aircraft carrier, the Fujian (Hull 18). Three types of aircraft recently completed their inaugural electromagnetic catapult-assisted takeoff and arrested landing trainings on the aircraft carrier.(eng.chinamil.com.cn/Photo by Ju Zhenhua) As aviation equipment advances toward lighter, higher-performance and multifunctional designs, 3D printing is emerging as a key technology for overcoming traditional manufacturing constraints. A key laboratory at AVIC Shenyang Aircraft Design and Research Institute, the developer of China's J-35 series fighter jets, has made breakthroughs in the practical application of 3D printing in aircraft development, according to a WeChat post by the Aviation Industry Corporation of China (AVIC) on Saturday. In traditional aircraft structural development, design and manufacturing are often disconnected. This approach can lead to development delays, excessive weight and cost overruns, making it difficult to meet the growing demand for lightweight, high-efficiency, long-lasting, multifunctional and cost-effective aircraft structures that can be developed rapidly. The advances in 3D printing technology at the Key Laboratory of Aviation Science and Technology for Novel Aircraft Structures under AVIC's Shenyang Aircraft Design and Research Institute are helping overcome the constraints of conventional manufacturing, enabling greater design flexibility and more efficient aircraft structural development, according to the release. AVIC's Shenyang Aircraft Design and Research Institute, China's first aircraft design and research institute, has undertaken the development of more than 40 major aviation equipment models across five series, including the J-8, J-11, J-15, J-35 and unmanned aircraft, according to people.com.cn. "With no need for molds, rapid production capabilities and the ability to fabricate complex structures, 3D printing plays an important role in aircraft development. It enables the integration of design and manufacturing, as well as structure and function, giving designers greater freedom," Cui Can, deputy director of the laboratory, was quoted by the AVIC release as saying. Cui added that 3D printing serves as a key accelerator, particularly during the prototyping of new aircraft, allowing a wide range of innovative structural designs to be rapidly turned into physical components for testing and evaluation. 3D printing technology is driving the manufacturing of large aircraft structures toward greater integration. In recent years, the laboratory has achieved breakthroughs in developing primary load-bearing aircraft structures, successfully producing an integrated structural component measuring more than five meters in length using 3D printing technology. Located in the aircraft's central fuselage, the component primarily serves to bear and transfer structural loads, according to AVIC. Installed inside an aircraft's air intake, the 3D-printed multifunctional annular heat exchanger integrates heat transfer, air extraction, load-bearing and maintenance functions. With the help of 3D printing technology, the research team also incorporated manufacturing requirements into the design process from the outset, developing complex internal flow channels that increase the heat transfer surface area while reducing the component's weight. Turning a successfully printed laboratory prototype into a component suitable for actual aircraft applications required overcoming major challenges in manufacturing and engineering validation. To address thermal stress, deformation and cracking during the printing of large components, the team developed an innovative process combining segmented component printing and additive fusion joining. To overcome difficulties in finishing the intricate internal channels of the annular heat exchanger, the researchers independently developed a specialized magnetic grinding device. By placing fine steel needles inside the flow channels and controlling their movement with an external magnetic field, the device enables the needles to slide, tumble and polish the internal surfaces without damaging the structure. Over more than two decades, the laboratory has pursued a path of innovation, progressing from technological exploration to engineering applications and from individual breakthroughs to the development of comprehensive technological capabilities. To date, it has successfully applied six additive manufacturing processes, 13 types of metal materials and 19 categories of 3D-printed structural components in aircraft development programs, said the release. The team has established a comprehensive technological development framework encompassing the incubation of novel structural concepts, breakthroughs in key technologies and engineering development. These efforts have helped overcome technical bottlenecks in aircraft development and advance innovation in aircraft structural technologies. The continued advancement and wider application of 3D printing technology have made innovative structural concepts a reality, including large-scale integrated structures, topology-optimized configurations, functionally graded composite structures and the integration of structural and functional capabilities. These advances are expected to enhance the overall performance and quality of airframe structures while supporting China's pursuit of self-reliance and strength in aviation science and technology. Global Times

item.title: Chinese Embassy slams baseless accusations against Chinese firms in Mexico, urges US business representative to stop interfering
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-14 12:27:00
An aerial view shows containers stacked on a cargo ship at the Port of Lázaro Cárdenas in Michoacán, Mexico, on April 25, 2025. Photo: VCG A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Mexico said accusations by Larry Rubin, president of the American Society of Mexico, that Chinese companies operating in Mexico are interfering in Mexico's sovereignty are entirely baseless. Rubin had urged the Mexican government to review the operations of Chinese companies, including Huawei in Mexico, and the spokesperson noted the Chinese Enterprises Association in Mexico has issued a strong response statement. China and Mexico are old friends and good partners who treat each other with mutual respect and equality. China has consistently required Chinese companies operating overseas to abide by local laws and regulations, respect local customs and fulfill their social responsibilities, the embassy said in a post on its official WeChat account on Saturday. Chinese companies investing and operating in Mexico have helped create local jobs, promote industrial development and support Mexico's modernization. They are participants in and contributors to mutually beneficial cooperation between the two countries, according to the statement. From advocating restrictions on trade with China during the review of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA), to urging Mexico to distance itself from China and other BRICS countries, Rubin has repeatedly sought to dictate whom Mexico should engage and cooperate with. Now, under the pretext of defending Mexico's sovereignty, he has once again smeared Chinese companies without any basis. Such actions are precisely what shows disrespect for Mexico's sovereignty, the spokesperson said. Mexico has the right to independently choose its partners. No ill-informed individual has the authority to dictate its choices. We urge people like Rubin to stop using fabricated allegations to disrupt normal China-Mexico cooperation and to stop interfering in Mexico's sovereignty with a condescending, self-righteous attitude, said the spokesperson. Global Times

item.title: Mutual growth of foreign firms, Chinese market is setting an example for openness in the Asia-Pacific: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-14 00:35:00
Lujiazui Photo:VCG In recent days, new developments of two long-established multinational corporations in the Chinese market have drawn the attention of Bloomberg, Reuters and other international media outlets. In October, German car brand Volkswagen saw its new-energy vehicle (NEV) deliveries in China surge by nearly 350 percent year-on-year, exceeding 28,000 units - a new monthly record. Meanwhile, US financial firm Citigroup views Chinese enterprises "going global" as a significant growth opportunity, with its China-related business posting double-digit growth for many consecutive years. For this manufacturing giant and this Wall Street bank, what they gained in China are more than just orders, but greater capabilities. While it was once common to hear that foreign firms viewed China merely as a "contract manufacturing hub," they now prefer to view the country as a vibrant "innovation workshop" - an environment where companies from diverse backgrounds engage in healthy competition and mutual learning, driving both technological iteration and the enhancement of global competitiveness. As one of the first multinational corporations to enter the Chinese market, Volkswagen must have gained a profound understanding of the unique value this market holds. Faced with a 30-percent decline in vehicle deliveries during the first three quarters of this year, the company chose to partner with XPeng to co-develop an all-new electronic and electrical architecture, collaborated with Horizon Robotics to address gaps in its intelligent driving capabilities, and established its largest R&D hub outside of Germany in Hefei. The intense competitive landscape and rapidly evolving consumer demands in China are compelling a century-old automotive giant like Volkswagen to continuously recalibrate its strategy and strengthen its core competencies, ensuring it avoids the risk of "atrophy" in the face of global competition. More importantly, the significance of the Chinese market for corporate development has long transcended the notion of a mere "fitness regimen." An increasing number of multinational corporations have completed a comprehensive evolution in China, ranging from technical adaptation and trial-and-error experimentation with business models to the complete restructuring of their operational systems. The new products, technologies, and business models refined here have not only enabled these firms to secure a firm foothold in China but have also been exported to global markets, granting them a distinct, competitive edge on the international stage. This transition from simply "benefiting in China" to "growing up in China" represents one of the most vivid new opportunities that the process of Chinese modernization offers to the global economy. This phenomenon, where a company coexists and co-develops with the market, is an inevitable outcome of the ongoing evolution of the Chinese innovation ecosystem. Take Volkswagen's transformation as an example: through partnerships with local firms, the company has become deeply embedded in the innovation network of China's NEV industry, rapidly addressing its own capability gaps for the era of intelligent mobility. The mature, refined technical solutions developed here are now being considered to upgrade vehicle models back in Europe. There are many more similar stories: Adient has rolled out product plans developed in its Chongqing R&D center to its 180 manufacturing sites worldwide, while Siemens Healthineers has exported over 150 products manufactured locally in China to more than 150 countries and regions. "What is learned in China is being monetized globally" - this has become a shared consensus among multinational corporate executives in their private discussions. Even more noteworthy is that a number of service-oriented multinational corporations are upgrading their own operational capabilities as they follow the global expansion of Chinese industries. Citigroup's strategic shift serves as a prime example: While foreign banks previously entered China primarily to serve multinational firms expanding into the Chinese market, they must now grasp the global strategic logic of Chinese new-energy enterprises, navigate the financial flow regulations of cross-border e-commerce, and tailor their services to the localized operational needs of Chinese companies in emerging markets. These capabilities, honed within the Chinese market, have, in turn, become unique advantages that allow these institutions to broaden their service reach on a global scale. This two-way empowerment has moved beyond the traditional, one-way flow of expertise from foreign firms to China, fostering a new landscape where Chinese and foreign enterprises learn from and support one another as they jointly explore global markets. Viewed through the lens of the 2026 APEC meeting in Shenzhen, the symbiotic practices currently unfolding in the Chinese market serve as a compelling illustration of the three key priorities championed by this year's APEC: openness, innovation, and cooperation. Industrial interaction within the Chinese market has transcended traditional frameworks; market participants from diverse backgrounds no longer function merely as isolated links in a supply chain. Instead, they engage in deep collaboration within an open innovation ecosystem - learning from one another through robust competition, jointly refining new technologies and business models, and ultimately cultivating fresh, globally-oriented competitiveness. This pragmatic experience, forged within the Chinese market, offers a tangible, actionable model for the Asia-Pacific region as it seeks to dismantle technical barriers, strengthen industrial chain resilience, and achieve more inclusive, shared prosperity. Today's global economy remains overshadowed by geopolitical conflicts, rising protectionism, and lackluster growth momentum. Many are anxious about the rhetoric surrounding "decoupling" and "severing supply chains" and concerned about the fragmentation of global markets. As a pivotal pole in the global economic landscape characterized by both substantial scale and a dynamic capacity for innovation, China neither forms exclusive, closed-off circles nor seeks a "winner-takes-all" unipolar advantage. Instead, through the continuous opening of its market and its commitment to innovation-driven development, China provides a platform for enterprises from all nations to grow together. As successive waves of multinational corporations return to the global marketplace, armed with new capabilities honed in China, they bring with them not only more efficient technologies and business models, but also a fundamental development philosophy that openness fosters progress, and cooperation catalyzes innovation. This represents the long-term value that the Chinese market contributes to the global economy - a value that transcends short-term gains.

item.title: It's Jensen Huang today. Who is next? Washington's list of targets may keep growing
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13 11:33:00
Nvidia's co-founder Jensen Huang Photo: VCG Jensen Huang, one of the most prominent figures in the global AI boom, has resigned. The immediate trigger, as presented in public, was a series of reports about his private life. But from the initial reports in the New York Times to the intense coverage across US media, the controversy has become about far more than a personal matter. Huang's affair was framed from the outset as a matter of US national security. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer wrote in an X post, "Despite Jensen Huang's resignation, Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk." This is a pattern worth watching closely amid the current US climate of technological competition with China. First, an individual case is used to ignite public debate; then the framework of "national security" is invoked to elevate it into an issue of systemic risk. In today's Washington, "national security" can sometimes be invoked without reference to a concrete, verifiable threat, becoming a narrative tool that can be applied to prominent ethnic Chinese professionals operating at the intersection of US-China tech competition. The Huang case illustrates this pattern starkly: he lobbied for chip exports to China - a move that could be portrayed as potentially endangering national security; he reportedly had a personal relationship with a woman suspected by US intelligence of having ties to Chinese intelligence - another "potential national security concern;" and he wielded influence in Washington while maintaining business ties with China - again, grounds for raising "national security concerns." The word "may" is the key. It allows suspicion to be cast without establishing that wrongdoing has occurred or reaching a verdict. In this climate, a combination of Chinese identity and political circumstances can be enough to turn a celebrated business leader into a perceived security risk. The more accomplished and influential a person is, and the more centrally positioned they are between China and the US, the more vulnerable they may become to being singled out in the name of "national security." More alarming is the way this is reinforced by a broader narrative that demonizes China. China is cast as a strategic competitor of the US, while "national security precautions" imposed on the entire Chinese community are being heightened to an unprecedented degree. "The Jensen Huang affair exposes corporate America's China problem" - read a headline by The Hill. But this problem was not created by China; it reflects a contradiction within the US itself. On one hand, the US relies on the creativity and expertise of top Chinese talent; on the other, it increasingly treats them as potential security threats. It needs Nvidia's technology and global competitiveness, yet it does not want the company to make its own commercial decisions about the Chinese market. That is the real contradiction. This contradiction will not stop with Jensen Huang alone. The next target could well be other tech entrepreneurs unwilling to fully align with Washington's political agenda - including those who might argue that the US should win by running faster rather than by tripping up its opponents. In the current US political environment, ordinary business logic has come to be seen as "politically incorrect." Entrepreneurs are being forced to fight on two fronts at once: the technology race in the global market, and political scrutiny in Washington. Many in Silicon Valley will probably have to weigh every decision carefully: asking not whether they have done anything wrong, but whether their business decisions involving China and the US might one day be recast as "national security risks." It's Jensen Huang today. Who is next? Perhaps Washington is already looking for the answer.

item.title: Why becoming a 'gatekeeper' for US protectionism is not in Mexico's interest
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13 00:27:00
US Mexico Illustration: Xia Qing/GT Washington has erected a wall of protectionism around the globe, and Mexico is eager to pass it more bricks, helping plug the "loopholes." But the higher this wall rises, the more likely it is to hem in Mexico itself, constraining not only its development prospects but also its independence in shaping trade policy. According to Reuters, Luis Rosendo Gutierrez, Mexico's deputy economy minister for foreign trade, said on Wednesday that the Mexican government had tightened traceability measures with industry to ensure that no steel from China or other countries is rerouted through its territory into the US by exploiting Mexico's trade preferences. Meanwhile, Mexico is urging Washington to ease tariffs on Mexican steel, aluminum and automobiles. Jiang Shixue, a distinguished professor at Hangzhou Normal University, told the Global Times that Mexico's move is rooted in its economic predicament created by strong dependence on the US. Facing US tariff pressure and uncertainty surrounding the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement review, Mexico hopes that aligning itself with Washington's restrictions on trade with China will win concessions from the US. Since 2025, Mexico has repeatedly followed the US to announce measures to impose tariffs on imports from China and other countries without free-trade agreements. It seems that Mexico is actively standing guard at the door on Washington's behalf. While other countries may justify trade barriers as necessary to protect their own industries, Mexico's restrictions appear to be protecting the interests of a "third party." In effect, Mexico risks turning itself into a gatekeeper for Washington's protectionism. This could end up as a potential "Faustian bargain." Mexico hopes to sacrifice part of its economic and trade cooperation with China in exchange for US concessions on tariffs and trade. But it may discover that what it surrenders far outweighs what it could gain. On the one hand, Washington is unlikely to abandon its trade pressure on Mexico. On the other, Mexico risks sacrificing long-term industrial cooperation, supply chain diversification and, ultimately, its economic sovereignty. According to Gutierrez, the country has already reduced steel and aluminum imports from countries including China, South Korea and India, by about 30 percent. Zhou Mi, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation, pointed out that manufacturing is a pillar of Mexico's economy, and steel and aluminum are essential inputs for industries such as auto manufacturing and machinery. Cutting imports of these materials could further aggravate supply pressures on Mexican manufacturers, disrupting production and undermining supply chain stability. More importantly, if Mexico can readily change its trade policies under external pressure, other countries may begin to question the stability and predictability of its investment and trade environment, he added. Once policy predictability is undermined, the price Mexico pays could go far beyond the immediate costs of tariffs. Just one day before the report, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum stressed that respect for sovereignty and cooperation free from subordination "are non-negotiable" tenets of Mexico's relations with the US. True sovereignty should not be confined to political rhetoric. It should be reflected in a country's ability to independently choose its trading partners, allocate resources according to its development needs and formulate its own economic and trade policies. In an increasingly interconnected global economy, broader international partnerships give countries greater room to maneuver amid external uncertainties. Canada, also deeply integrated into the North American economic system, has not abandoned efforts to diversify its trading partners and is actively seeking to expand cooperation with China and other economies to get rid of its dependence on the US. America's trade wall is America's choice. Mexico has no reason to turn it into its own barrier to development. What Mexico truly needs is not to become another brick in Washington's protectionist wall, but to safeguard its economic sovereignty, preserve its ability to connect with global markets and participate in international industrial chains. Otherwise, in trying to please Washington, Mexico risks cutting off its nose to spite its face.
